newsitem.title: USA: Shuttle crew to haul space telescope on board.
newsitem.headline: Shuttle crew to haul space telescope on board.

text.p: NASA managers wrestled with contingency plans for fixing a jammed hatch on Tuesday as the crew of the Columbia prepared to retrieve a star-gazing telescope following the shuttle through space.

The five-member crew stowed equipment and fired steering thrusters to ready the shuttle to recapture the Orfeus-Spas orbiting telescope, trailing at a distance of 26 miles. It was to be retrieved at 3:26 a.m. EST (0826 GMT) on Wednesday.

The mission was extended by a day to give the telescope, a U.S.-German project, more time to gather data on interstellar matter in a study on the life cycles of stars. Columbia was scheduled to return to Earth on Friday, landing at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre shortly after 8 a.m. EST (1300 GMT).

Orfeus-Spas, released from the shuttle shortly after launch two weeks ago, has been one of the success stories of a mission marred by a jammed airlock hatch that forced the cancellation of two planned spacewalks.

NASA officials described the retrieval of Orfeus-Spas as routine. Thrusters will manoeuvre Columbia into place and astronaut Tom Jones will use the shuttle's robot arm to pluck the satellite from space and deposit it in the payload bay.

"The Orfeus-Spas is equipped with a grapple fixture. He'll reach out and grab the telescope," NASA spokeswoman Eileen Hawley said. But if something goes wrong with the retrieval, the retraction of antennas or the robot arm, one of the standard procedures, a spacewalk or "extra vehicular activity" (EVA) in NASA jargon, to fix the problem may not be an option.

With two mission spacewalks cancelled because of the stuck hatch, NASA managers were discussing contingencies in case of emergency. "If something went wrong in the retrieval, you could leave the satellite there. If there was a problem with the robot arm you could jettison that," Hawley said.
"Clearly that's not something we want to do. Those are expensive pieces of equipment," she added.

During a news conference from the shuttle late on Monday, astronaut Tammy Jernigan said if an emergency arose the crew would have to make another attempt to get the hatch open. "If we got into that very remote possibility then we would work very hard to get that hatch open and very hard to get it sealed back," she said.

But shuttle commander Ken Cockrell said the possibility of an emergency spacewalk was remote because of contingencies for the failure of the payload bay doors or the robot arm. "It actually hasn't crossed our mind really that an EVA that perhaps can't be done would be required," he said.
NASA engineers remained mystified by the failure of the airlock hatch, which prevented the astronauts from leaving the shuttle on Thursday to perform their spacewalks.

Experts examined hatches on the shuttles Atlantis and Discovery to try to find similar problems and ground engineers dismantled hatches and gear cranks to figure out how they could jam. And the astronauts aboard Columbia videotaped the stuck hatch and sent the tape back to Earth for study.
But NASA could not find a reason for the hatch failure, the first in the 15-year history of the shuttle programme.
